A string gives its bytes: UTF-8, with the escapes \n \t \r \0 \\ \' \". dw 0x1234, $ Words, low byte first. resb 16 Reserves 16 zero bytes, which are DAT. resw 8 Reserves 8 zero words. times 4 nop Repeats an instruction or data line. $ is the address of the times line in every repeat. align 4 Pads with 00 (DAT) to a multiple of 4. The power of 2 is required. The zeros of resb, resw, and align are DAT: code that runs into them dies. Put data after the code, behind a jump (the linter warns: dat-in-code).

records.heading: Constants and macros
records.text: directive does STRIDE equ 4 A named number, from any constant expression. It can name labels: SIZE equ end - start. %define GAP 0x100 A one-line text macro, no parameters. It applies from its line on. org 0 Accepted; must be 0. Bots are position independent. bits 16 Accepted, and ignored.

records.heading: Labels
records.text: name: defines a label at the address of the line. The colon may be left out before a statement word: size equ 4, msg db 1. .name is local to the last label without a dot, so each phase can have its own .loop. Its full name is scan.again. $ is the address of the line, and $$ is 0. jmp $ spins in place.

records.heading: Size and jump words
records.text: word does mov word [bx], 0 byte and word give the size of a memory operand when no register does. jmp short $+2 short forces rel8. jmp near $+2 near forces rel16. add ax, strict word 5 strict keeps the field size given: here an imm16 where an imm8 would do.

records.heading: Not supported
records.text: x16c leaves out what a one-file, one-segment bot has no use for, with an error that says so (unsupported): sections, extern and global, multi-line %macro, %if, %include, incbin, segment registers, far jumps, and 32-bit registers. See diagnostics.

records.heading: expressions
records.text: Anywhere a number goes, an expression can: an immediate, a displacement, a jump target, a dw, an equ, a times count. The assembler folds each one to a number (ISA §6.1).

records.heading: Numbers
records.text: write value is 123 0x007B (123) decimal 0x1F 0x001F (31) hexadecimal 1Fh 0x001F (31) hexadecimal, NASM suffix: it must start with a digit (0FFh) 0b1010 0x000A (10) binary 'A' 0x0041 (65) a character: its code -7 0xFFF9 (65529) a negative number, as 16 bits

records.heading: Operators
records.text: C operators and C precedence, all left to right. From the first to bind to the last: operators are -x +x ~x negate, plus, flip every bit * / % multiply, divide, remainder + - add, subtract << >> shift left, shift right & and ^ xor | or ( ) group expression value because 2 + 3 * 4 0x000E (14) * binds first (2 + 3) * 4 0x0014 (20) parentheses first 1 << 4 | 1 0x0011 (17) << binds before | 0xFF & ~0x0F 0x00F0 (240) ~ flips every bit of 0x000F -5 / 3 0xFFFF (65535) / is signed and rounds toward 0, as in C -5 % 3 0xFFFE (65534) % takes the sign of the left side, as in C -1 >> 4 0xFFFF (65535) >> is arithmetic: the sign stays (0x8000 * 4) / 8 0x4000 (16384) the math is exact, and wraps to 16 bits once, at the end 0x10000 + 5 0x0005 (5) a value wraps to 16 bits NASM differs: its /, %, and >> are unsigned (its signed ones are //, %%, and >>>, which x16c does not have). See 8086 divergences.

records.heading: Labels and $
records.text: A label is a number: its offset from the start of the bot. So end - start is the size of the code between them, and $ is the offset of the current line. A label is an offset, not an address in the core: mov ax, [label] reads the absolute address label. Add the base: [bx+label] (see memory model).

records.heading: Errors
records.text: A name no label or equ defines is undefined-symbol; a division by 0 is div-zero; an equ defined through itself is circular-equ; a value too big for its field is out-of-range. A byte field takes -256..255, a sign-extended byte -128..127, and a word any value, wrapped.

records.heading: diagnostics
records.text: The assembler gives errors, and a bot with an error has no bytes. The linter gives warnings about a bot that assembles but may not do what its author means; each comes with a fix. Each has a code, which the editor shows beside the message: 3:9: error: jump out of range [jump-out-of-range]. Each example below gives its code and no other (after a %name and a %strategy line), and the quote under it is the message the editor shows for it.

records.heading: absolute-address

[0x0100] is an absolute address: a fixed place in the core, not in this bot, which the loader places anywhere (ISA §6.4) Fix: for the bot's own data, add a base register: [bx+0x0100], with bx from the base idiom call .here / .here: pop bx / sub bx, .here

records.heading: dat-in-code
records.text: warning, from the lint. DAT that code falls into: dat, or the zeros of resb, resw, and align. the line before falls through into dat: the process dies there Fix: end the code before it with a jmp, or move the data after the code

records.heading: size-near-cap
records.text: warning, from the lint. A bot of 90% of maxBytes or more. the bot is 470 bytes, 91% of the limit of 512 (42 left); it reaches 90% on this line Fix: keep room for changes: rel8 jumps, inc and dec for small steps, fewer times repeats, less data

records.heading: no-strategy
records.text: warning, from the lint. No %strategy, or an empty one. no %strategy Fix: say in one line how the bot fights: %strategy "..."; the arena and the hills show it

records.heading: hlt-in-code
records.text: warning, from the lint. A hlt that the bot runs. hlt is the first instruction: the bot halts itself at once Fix: to park a process, spin with jmp $; keep a bomb template after a jmp, where no code runs into it

records.heading: uninitialized-di
records.text: warning, from the lint. A string instruction that uses di before any line sets di. movsb uses di, and no line before it sets di: di starts at 0, a fixed place in the core Fix: set di first, from the base register: lea di, [bx+target]

records.heading: 8086 divergences
records.text: x16c is real 8086 machine code: every instruction the assembler writes is the 8086 encoding, ndisasm -b16 reads a bot, and any 8086 reference holds for it. It differs in three places, all on purpose (ISA §9).

records.heading: 00 is DAT
records.text: On the 8086, 00 /r is add r/m8, r8. Here 00 is dat, whatever byte follows, because empty core must kill. So add byte [bx], al is an error: this form encodes as 0x00 (DAT) and is unavailable; use add <mem8>, imm8 or a word operation A byte add of two registers takes the other encoding, 02 /r: add al, bl is 02 C3.

records.heading: 60, 61, and 62 are spl
records.text: On the 8086, 60..62 are undefined; the 80186 made them pusha, popa, and bound. Here they are spl: 60 cb, 61 cw, and 62 /0.

records.heading: No segments, interrupts, I/O, or timing
records.text: One flat 64 KB core. No segment registers, segment prefixes, or far jumps and calls: those bytes are undefined, and kill. hlt, int3, and every undefined opcode kill the process instead of stopping or trapping. There is no int n, in, out, cli, or sti. Every instruction takes one cycle. A rep instruction takes one cycle per iteration, and can be stopped between two, as an interrupt stops the 8086.

records.heading: Where the 8086 decides
records.text: Where the ISA leaves a behavior open, x16c does what the 8086 silicon does: push sp pushes the value of sp after the decrement; the 80286 and later push the value before. pop sp leaves sp holding the popped word. A shift count in cl is not masked to 5 bits, as later CPUs do: a count of 40 shifts 40 times. idiv kills on a quotient of -32768 (-128 for a byte), as the 8086 does. A shift or rotate by a count of 0 changes no flag, but writes its memory operand back. The flags the 8086 manual leaves undefined have fixed values: see flags.

records.heading: Where the assembler differs from NASM
records.text: nasm -f bin assembles most bots to the same bytes. Where the two differ, x16c gives an error instead of a guess, or these bytes: source x16c NASM why add al, bl 02 C3 00 D8 00 /r is DAT (ISA §9), so a byte add of two registers uses 02 /r. xchg bx, cx 87 CB 87 D9 The first operand goes in the ModR/M rm field, so the decoder gives the operands back in their order. xchg ax, ax 87 C0 90 90 is nop. start: add bx, start 83 C3 00 81 C3 00 00 x16c sizes a label like any number, so a small address takes the short form. NASM always gives a label 16 bits. start: mov ax, [bx+start] 8B 07 8B 87 00 00 The same rule for a displacement. The dwarf in Listing is 21 bytes, and 23 in NASM. a: add bx, (b - a) * 32b: 81 C3 80 00 83 C3 60 Pass 1 gives an unknown value the long form, where NASM guesses the short one. Only code whose size depends on itself can end differently. nopalign 4 90 00 00 00 90 90 90 90 align pads with 00, which is DAT (ISA §6.2). mov ax, -5 / 3 B8 FF FF B8 53 55 / is signed and truncates toward zero, as in C. NASM's / is unsigned; its signed one is //. mov ax, -5 % 3 B8 FE FF B8 02 00 % is signed and takes the sign of the dividend, as in C. NASM's % is unsigned; its signed one is %%. mov ax, -1 >> 63 B8 FF FF B8 01 00 >> is arithmetic. NASM's >> is logical; its arithmetic one is >>>. db 'a\n' 61 0A 61 5C 6E The escapes \n \t \r \0 \\ \' \" work in both quote styles. NASM has escapes only in backquotes. mov ax, 'é' B8 E9 00 B8 C3 A9 A one-character literal in an expression is its UTF-16 code. NASM uses its UTF-8 bytes. In db, both give the UTF-8 bytes.

records.heading: The imp
records.text: An imp is a bot that is its own copy. Its step is two bytes, movsw and nop: movsw copies the word it runs from (si) to the word after it (di) and moves si and di 2 bytes on, and nop steps onto the copy. Start here takes it apart line by line. It moves one byte a cycle, around the core, forever.

records.heading: Why an imp is hard to kill
records.text: A bomb that lands ahead of the imp is gone before the imp gets there: the imp writes its next word over it. A bomb behind it hits old copies that no process runs. A bomb kills it only when it lands on the bytes the imp runs next, in the cycle or two between the movsw that writes them and the step onto them.

records.heading: Why an imp seldom wins
records.text: An imp writes nothing but itself. It kills only when a rival's process runs into its trail: that process runs movsw with its own si and di, copies a word from somewhere to somewhere, and walks on until it meets a zero. So imps tie, and ties are worth 1 point of 3. These records play seeds 1 to 20 at hill rules (80,000 cycles), and swap the order each seed, as a match does: the bot on the left goes first at seed 1. seeds 1..20, hill rules record imp vs imp 0 W / 20 T / 0 L imp vs dwarf 2 W / 9 T / 9 L imp vs gate 0 W / 1 T / 19 L

records.heading: Imp rings
records.text: In Redcode, an imp ring is a few imps spaced evenly around the core, each copying itself onto the place of the next. In x16c each imp copies only itself, one word ahead, so a ring is simpler: several independent imps, spread out. A bomb that kills one leaves the others walking, and the bot lives until the last one is hit. The price is speed. A bot runs one instruction a cycle, whatever the count of its processes (see processes). With three imps, each imp runs every third cycle and moves a byte every 3 cycles, so a bomber has three times as long to hit each next word. The launch writes each imp as one word, 0x90A5: the bytes A5 90 in little-endian order. spl si starts the child with a copy of the parent's registers, so each child walks from its own si and di. The ring's record is no better than the imp's against a bomber. It is the same kind of bot, with spares: seeds 1..20, hill rules record imp-ring vs dwarf 3 W / 5 T / 12 L imp-ring vs stone 1 W / 8 T / 11 L imp-ring vs gate 0 W / 3 T / 17 L Try more imps: set THIRD equ 8192 and mov cx, 7. That is eight imps, an eighth of the core apart, each moving a byte every 8 cycles. Against the dwarf the record goes from 3 W / 5 T / 12 L to 5 W / 7 T / 8 L, and against the gate from 0 W / 3 T / 17 L to 1 W / 11 T / 8 L. Spares beat speed here, because the bombers need one hit per imp.

records.heading: What imps are for
records.text: Few bots win as imps. They are parts: a decoy that keeps a bot alive for a tie when its bombers are dead (stones), or a trail of non-zero bytes that keeps a scanner busy (hygiene). And every bomber must plan for them: an imp crosses a stride-4 bomb pattern often enough to live, so the answer is an imp gate or a solid carpet (stack tricks). See also: movsw and spl in the reference.

records.heading: The dwarf
records.text: A dwarf is a bomber: it walks through the core and writes a DAT (a zero word) every few bytes. A process that runs into a bomb dies. The gap between two bombs is the stride. The dwarf below uses a stride of 4 and walks backward, down from its own base. The loop is three instructions (sub, mov, loop) for one bomb, so the dwarf drops a bomb every 3 cycles. loop is the jump back and the lap counter in one: it takes 1 from cx and jumps while cx is not 0.

records.heading: What a stride hits
records.text: A bomb is a word: it zeros 2 bytes. With a stride of s bytes, one lap zeros 2 bytes of every s. An instruction survives the lap only if it fits in the s - 2 bytes between two bombs, so the stride sets the longest instruction a lap can miss. The dwarf's loop costs 3 cycles a bomb whatever the stride, so a longer stride laps the core faster. stride a lap zeros longest instruction a lap can miss cycles a lap (the dwarf's loop) 2 every byte none 98,271 3 2 bytes of 3 1 byte 65,514 4 2 bytes of 4 2 bytes 49,137 5 2 bytes of 5 3 bytes 39,309 8 2 bytes of 8 6 bytes: any instruction 24,570 A stride of 2 is a solid carpet, but its first lap does not end before a hill round does (80,000 cycles). A stride of 8 laps fast and can miss every instruction of a bot. Most bombers sit between: at stride 3 no instruction of 2 bytes or more survives a lap, at stride 4 none of 3 bytes or more, and a bot of more than a few instructions nearly always loses one. A missed instruction still hurts its bot. If a bomb takes the next instruction, the process dies when it gets there. If a bomb takes only a byte or two of a long instruction, the process runs the bytes that are left out of step with its code, and those seldom make sense for long. Unrolling makes the loop cheaper per bomb. Dwarf Wide writes 4 bombs a pass with 4 stores at fixed offsets from di, one sub, and one loop: 6 instructions for 4 bombs, 1.5 cycles a bomb, twice the dwarf's pace.

records.heading: Which strides hit every address
records.text: Take away the lap counter and let di run on around the core. After n bombs, di has moved n × s bytes, mod 65,536. It comes back to its start after 65,536 / g bombs, where g is the largest power of 2 that divides s (the greatest common divisor of s and 65,536). So: An odd stride (g = 1) visits every address. Given time, it bombs every word of the core, the bomber's own code too. A stride of 2 (g = 2) visits every even address. Word bombs cover the odd bytes, so it bombs every byte. A stride with g of 4 or more visits one address in g. The bombs land on 2 bytes of every g-byte block, the same 2 bytes each time, and never on the other g - 2.

records.heading: Which strides self-avoid
records.text: The core is a multiple of every power of 2, so a bomber with no lap counter comes back to where it started. If its own code sits on the bytes it bombs, it kills itself. It self-avoids only when its code fits in the g - 2 bytes that it never bombs: g - 2 bytes or less, placed between the bombs. The dwarf's 23 bytes need g of 32 or more. That is why the dwarf counts laps instead: at stride 4, a lap without the counter comes back to the dwarf and bombs its code. Try replacing loop .bomb with jmp .bomb (the linter warns that jmp lap is now unreachable). Run the dwarf alone in the debugger: di comes back around, a bomb lands on the dwarf's own loop, and it dies with dat in cycle 49,142. A bomber that self-avoids the Redcode way picks a stride of 32 and aims its bombs at the last 2 bytes of each 32-byte block. Its 19 bytes sit in the 30 that it never bombs, so it needs no counter and never stops: It lives alone for as long as you run it. But it zeros only 2 bytes of 32, and a bot of 30 bytes or less can sit in its gaps forever. The trade is density for safety, and density wins: seeds 1..20, hill rules record dwarf vs imp 14 W / 6 T / 0 L dwarf-wide vs imp 16 W / 4 T / 0 L Stride 32 vs imp 9 W / 10 T / 1 L Stride 32 vs dwarf 1 W / 6 T / 13 L

records.heading: Choosing a stride
records.text: Bomb density decides what you kill: stride 3 or 4 breaks nearly every bot that it passes over. Lap time decides when: a rival far away may run for most of a lap before the first bomb reaches it. Self-safety is the lap counter's job. Count the bombs in a lap so the last one lands just past your own body: LAP equ (0x10000 - SIZE) / STRIDE. Imps walk through a stride-4 pattern often enough to tie. Add an imp gate, or a stride of 2 (stack tricks has a fast one). See also: loop and mov in the reference.

records.heading: Several bombers in one bot
records.text: In Redcode, a stone is a small, fast bomber, often paired with an imp. In x16c a stone uses spl to run several bombers at once, each with its own stride, and often an imp as a decoy. The bombers share the bot's turn: a bot runs one instruction a cycle whatever it holds (see processes). So splitting does not bomb faster. It buys two things: Coverage. Two strides make two patterns. A sparse one laps the core fast and hits a rival early; a dense one follows and leaves no instruction of 3 bytes or more whole. Spares. A bomb kills one process. A bot with a bomber and a decoy still lives, for a tie, when its bomber is hit.

records.heading: Unrolled bombers
records.text: Each bomber of the stone is the dwarf's loop, unrolled: four stores at fixed offsets from di, then one sub and one loop. That is 6 instructions for 4 bombs, 1.5 cycles a bomb, where the dwarf's loop takes 3. The bomb comes from a register: mov [di], ax with ax = 0 is 2 bytes (3 with a displacement), where mov word [di], 0 is 4. Smaller code is a smaller target. Dwarf Wide is this loop at stride 3.

records.heading: The stone
records.text: The launcher is 5 instructions. spl si starts the decoy on an imp word a quarter of the core away, with the si and di it needs. spl sparse starts the second bomber, and the parent falls through to dense. From then on the three processes take turns, so each runs every third cycle. Alone at seed 1, the sparse bomber's first lap takes 23,749 cycles and the dense bomber's 54,997; the header's 27,000 is the sparse lap with the decoy imp still alive the whole way. The decoy walks into bombs sooner or later, and the bombers then share the turn two ways.

records.heading: Why a stone beats a scanner
records.text: A scanner reads one byte a cycle and carpets what it finds. The sparse bomber covers the core in under 24,000 cycles, so it usually reaches the scanner first, and stride 11 puts 4 bombs on the scanner's 43 bytes. But a stone loses to paper: paper has 64 processes in 64 places, and it copies faster than the stone can bomb them. seeds 1..20, hill rules record stone vs imp 15 W / 5 T / 0 L stone vs dwarf 16 W / 0 T / 4 L stone vs scanner 16 W / 0 T / 4 L stone vs paper 0 W / 8 T / 12 L Try deleting the line spl sparse. The stone keeps one bomber (the dense one) and the decoy. Against the imp its record goes from 15 W / 5 T / 0 L to 12 W / 8 T / 0 L: without the fast lap, more imps live to the cycle cap.

records.heading: Tuning a stone
records.text: Strides that share no factor make patterns that seldom meet. Bombs of stride 4 and stride 11 land on the same address once every 44 bytes. Order the spl lines so the process you most need starts first. Each child goes into the queue just ahead of its parent (see spl). The decoy is a cost. It takes one turn in three. It pays when the bombers die, and when its trail pulls a scanner away. Against an imp it costs wins: without spl si, the stone goes 17 W / 3 T / 0 L. See also: dwarves and stride math, and papers for the bots that stones lose to.

records.heading: Paper
records.text: A paper is a replicator. It copies its body to another place with rep movsw, starts a process in the copy with spl, and goes on to copy again. Each copy copies too, so the count of processes doubles until it reaches the process cap (64). From then on, every copy writes the paper's code over whatever it lands on, and spl does nothing (see the cap). A bomber must kill all 64 processes, in 64 places, while the survivors keep making more. It seldom does.

records.heading: What a copy costs
records.text: rep movsw runs one iteration a cycle, so a copy of the 34-byte paper takes 17 of its bot's turns. With the 4 instructions before it and the 3 after, a pass of the loop is 24 turns. Alone at seed 1, the first spl runs in cycle 26 and the bot holds 64 processes after 2,026 cycles. Each copy starts with the base idiom, so it finds its own base and runs as a new paper. xchg dl, dh starts each copy's path from its own base with the bytes swapped: a parent and its children walk different paths, and the copies spread over the core instead of piling up on one line.

records.heading: Why spl after rep movsw
records.text: A process that spl starts runs at once: the child goes into the queue just ahead of its parent, so it takes the bot's next turn. If paper started the copy before writing it, the child would run empty core. Try moving spl dx to the line just above rep movsw. Alone at seed 1, the first child starts in cycle 9, runs in cycle 10, finds a zero where its code should be, and dies with dat. Every child dies the same way, the bot keeps just its one process, and against the dwarf the record falls from 14 W / 6 T / 0 L to 7 W / 0 T / 13 L. Paper's order has a cost too. The copy takes 17 turns, and the parent is exposed for all of them: a bomb on the rep movsw kills the parent mid-copy, and the half-written copy never runs.

records.heading: Silk: spl first, safely
records.text: Silk starts the child first and writes the copy after, with a pad that makes it safe: Write a jmp $ pad (EB FE) where the copy will begin. spl to the pad. The child spins there, one jmp $ a turn. Copy the body from the top word down (std), so the last word written lands on the pad. The moment the copy is whole, its first word replaces the pad, and the child runs into a whole copy. If a bomb kills the parent mid-copy, the child still lives, spinning on its pad, so the bot lives too. The spinning children take turns too: while a copy is being written, its child spends a turn in each round of the queue on jmp $. Silk grows a little slower (64 processes after 2,213 cycles alone at seed 1, where paper takes 2,026) and wins a little less. It also loses less. seeds 1..20, hill rules record paper vs dwarf 14 W / 6 T / 0 L silk vs dwarf 11 W / 9 T / 0 L paper vs stone 13 W / 6 T / 1 L silk vs stone 5 W / 15 T / 0 L paper vs scanner 19 W / 1 T / 0 L paper vs silk 0 W / 20 T / 0 L

records.heading: What paper kills with
records.text: A paper kills by landing a copy on a rival's code, or with its one bomb a pass. A copy writes 34 bytes of paper over whatever is there. A rival's process then runs paper's bytes from wherever its ip is: from the copy's first byte, it becomes a paper for its own bot and lives; from the middle, it runs them out of step and seldom lasts. Two papers fill the core with copies of each other, and tie. Paper's threat is a bot that turns its numbers against it: the vampire holds its processes in a pit. See also: rep, movsw, and processes and cycles.

records.heading: Look, then bomb
records.text: A bomber spends most of its bombs on empty core. A scanner looks first: it reads the core for bytes that are not zero, and bombs only where it finds them. Empty core is zero, so a non-zero byte is code (or a trail, or a decoy). When the scan is cheap and the bomb is heavy, the scanner kills with few bombs.

records.heading: repe scasb and repne scasb
records.text: scasb compares al with the byte at di, sets the flags as cmp does, and steps di (down after std, up after cld). With a prefix it repeats, one iteration a cycle, while cx is not 0 and the condition holds: prefix repeats while with al = 0 it stops at repe (repz) the byte equals al (ZF = 1) the first byte that is not zero: code repne (repnz) the byte differs from al (ZF = 0) the first byte that is zero: a gap So a scanner that hunts code uses repe scasb with al = 0. repne scasb is the scan for one known byte: set al to it, and the scan stops on the first match. Hybrid uses repne scasb the other way round, to find a zero in a guard that should hold none. After the scan, check why it stopped. ZF = 0 means it found a byte that is not al; ZF = 1 means cx ran out first. Either way di has already stepped past the byte, so the hit is at di + 1 (after std) or di - 1 (after cld).

records.heading: The scanner
records.text: One register does the whole bomb: ax = 0 is both the byte the scan passes over and the word the carpet writes. std makes the scan and the carpet both walk down. The carpet is 16 words, 32 bytes of zeros, from 18 bytes above the hit: the scan goes down, so the first byte it meets of an imp is the imp's newest word, and the imp's next word is just above it.

records.heading: Self-skip
records.text: The scan wraps around the core and comes back to the scanner itself. Its own code is not zero, so the scan stops on it. The scanner must know its own body and not bomb it. It also must not bomb near it: a carpet that starts 18 bytes above a hit reaches down, and up, past the hit. The check is one subtraction and one unsigned compare. dx = hit - (base - BELOW) is small when the hit is in the band from BELOW bytes under the base to ABOVE bytes over the end, and huge otherwise, because a hit under the band wraps to a number near 65,536. So cmp dx, BELOW + SIZE + ABOVE then jae bomb bombs only hits outside the band. For a hit inside it, the scanner starts the scan again from under its own body. Try replacing jae bomb with jmp bomb: no self-skip (the linter warns that the next lines are unreachable). Run it alone. The scan reads the whole core, one byte a cycle, finds its own body, carpets it, and dies with undefined in cycle 65,497.

records.heading: Speed
records.text: A byte a cycle is slow. The scan needs 65,536 cycles to read the whole core: most of a hill round (80,000 cycles). A bomber that is far away gets time to find the scanner first, which is why a stone usually does. And paper has 64 copies in 64 places: the scanner finds and carpets them one at a time, while the rest make more. seeds 1..20, hill rules record scanner vs imp 20 W / 0 T / 0 L scanner vs dwarf 9 W / 0 T / 11 L scanner vs stone 3 W / 0 T / 17 L scanner vs paper 0 W / 2 T / 18 L A faster scanner samples. The vampire reads one word every 16 bytes: mov dx, [di] and three or dx, [di-K] test 4 words in 4 instructions, and it runs repe scasw only where a sample was not zero. With the jump and the step, it passes 64 bytes of empty core in 7 instructions, where repe scasb takes 64. The cost is blind spots: a bot of 14 bytes or less can fall between the sampled words. Long bots and trails cannot.

records.heading: Decoys
records.text: A scanner stops at every non-zero byte, whether it is a rival's code or not. A decoy is non-zero bytes that are not code: noise that a scanner carpets and a sampler bites, for nothing. Hygiene measures what noise buys against each kind of scanner.

records.heading: Hybrid
records.text: Hybrid scans and carpets as the scanner does, and keeps a guard: 16 bytes of 0xFF, 768 bytes over its body. A bot cannot read who owns a byte, but it can read a byte, so every 128 bytes of scan it checks the guard with repne scasb (al = 0): a zero in the guard is a bomb, and a bomber walking down the core is 768 bytes away. Then it turns to paper. It scores 17 W / 3 T / 0 L against the dwarf, where the plain scanner scores 9 W / 0 T / 11 L. seeds 1..20, hill rules record hybrid vs dwarf 17 W / 3 T / 0 L See also: scasb, repe, repne, and stosw in the reference.

records.heading: Capture, not kill
records.text: A bomb kills the process that runs it. A fang does worse: it is a jump, written over a rival's code, into a pit that the vampire owns. A rival's process that runs the fang jumps into the pit and stays there, running the vampire's code on its own bot's turns. In Redcode the pit is a loop of SPL and JMP; the captured bot's processes spin in it until the vampire closes it and they die together. Capture beats a kill against bots with many processes. A held process still takes its turn and its slot, so a held paper runs pit code instead of copying, and its spl fills its own queue with more held processes.

records.heading: Building a jump at run time
records.text: A jump in the core must hold the distance to its target, and the vampire does not know, when it assembles, where a fang will land. So it builds each fang as it bites: the byte E9 (jmp rel16) and a 16-bit distance. jmp rel16 jumps to the address of the next instruction plus rel16. A fang is 3 bytes, so a fang at address f jumps to f + 3 + rel16, and to reach a pit at address p: The vampire works this out once for the top fang, dx = (bx + pit - 3) - di, and then writes the fangs downward, 3 bytes apart. Each fang is 3 bytes lower, so its distance to the pit is 3 bytes more: add dx, 3.

records.heading: The pit
records.text: A bitten process runs the pit with its own registers and for its own bot. So everything it does, it does to its own side: spl .hold starts another held process, until its bot is at the cap. The bot's free slots fill with processes that do nothing useful. mov word [bx+si], 0 zeros the word at bx + si. A bot in the house style keeps its base in bx, so a held process zeros its own bot's home, 64 bytes of it, over and over. The loop never ends by itself. At the end of each scan lap the vampire writes a zero word over .hold: every held process runs a DAT on its next pass and dies. A bot whose processes were all held is dead. The pit writes only zeros, and only through the bitten bot's own registers. The vampire's own body is not in reach of that write unless the bitten bot's bx points at it.

records.heading: Records
records.text: The vampire beats bombers and scanners: it samples fast (64 bytes of empty core in 7 instructions, see scanners), and one bite turns a rival's own processes against it. Paper is the bad match: its copies are everywhere, one of them lands on the vampire sooner or later, and the vampire has no spares. seeds 1..20, hill rules record vampire vs imp 19 W / 1 T / 0 L vampire vs dwarf 16 W / 0 T / 4 L vampire vs scanner 19 W / 0 T / 1 L vampire vs paper 4 W / 0 T / 16 L vampire vs silk 6 W / 4 T / 10 L Try deleting the line mov word [bx+pit.hold], 0, so the pit never closes. Held bots now live to the cycle cap, and wins turn into ties: against the dwarf the record goes from 16 W / 0 T / 4 L to 12 W / 4 T / 4 L, and against paper from 4 W / 0 T / 16 L to 0 W / 12 T / 8 L.

records.heading: Pitfalls
records.text: The pit is code in your body. A rival that reads your fangs finds the pit address in them. Keep the pit small. Fangs are not zero. A bite leaves 48 bytes of non-zero code in the core, which another scanner stops on. The pit relies on the victim's bx. A bot that keeps its base elsewhere is held, but the pit zeros some other place. Imps are hard to bite. An imp writes over a fang in its path before it gets there, so only a fang written on the bytes the imp runs next catches it. The bite starts 17 bytes above the hit, where an imp walking up goes next, and that is enough: 19 W / 1 T / 0 L. See also: jmp, spl, and position independence.

records.heading: The problem
records.text: A bomber with a stride of 3 or more leaves gaps, and an imp moves through the gaps: it writes its next word over any bomb ahead of it. So a dwarf ties imps it should beat, and a bot that ties everything scores points on a hill. An imp gate is a cheap answer: one word of the core that the bot keeps changing, on the path an imp must take.

records.heading: How a gate kills
records.text: An imp built on movsw and nop walks up the core, so it meets a word under a bot's body before the body. The gate is such a word: the bot decrements it again and again, as fast as it can. The imp writes its next word, then runs it two cycles later (see imps). If the gate's dec lands in between, the imp runs a word one less than it wrote: the imp's word at the gate after dec runs as then A5 90 (movsw, nop) A4 90 movsb, nop copies 1 byte, not 2: the imp runs into a half-written word and dies in the gap 90 A5 (nop, movsw) 8F A5 pop with ModR/M A5 8F /4 is undefined: it dies at once Which row happens depends on where the imp started: an imp whose words are one byte out of step with the gate meets the second row. Either way the imp dies under the body.

records.heading: The gate
records.text: times 8 dec word [bx-GATE] is 8 copies of one 3-byte instruction, so the gate process decrements on 8 of its 9 turns; the ninth is the jmp. The gate and the bomber share the bot's turn, so the gate word changes on 8 cycles in 18. An imp's word sits on the gate for 2 cycles, and a dec nearly always lands in them. The bomber's first bomb is at bx - 9 and the pattern steps down by 9, so bombs land 9, 18, 27 bytes under the base: never on the gate at 16. seeds 1..20, hill rules record gate vs imp 20 W / 0 T / 0 L gate vs imp-ring 18 W / 2 T / 0 L gate vs dwarf 14 W / 0 T / 6 L imp vs gate 0 W / 1 T / 19 L Try replacing spl bomb with jmp bomb. The gate process never starts, and Gate is a plain bomber at stride 9. Against the imp the record falls from 20 W / 0 T / 0 L to 15 W / 5 T / 0 L, and against the imp ring from 18 W / 2 T / 0 L to 9 W / 5 T / 6 L. A slower gate still works: with times 1 in place of times 8, it scores 18 W / 2 T / 0 L against the imp.

records.heading: What a gate costs
records.text: A process. The gate takes half of the bot's turns, so the bomber runs at half speed. Imps only. The gate guards the way an imp comes: up, from under the body. Bombs, scans, and copies come from anywhere, and the gate does nothing about them. Its own code. times 8 is 24 bytes, a target for bombs and a find for scanners. times 1 is 3. See also: imps and imp rings, and dec in the reference.

records.heading: The stack is core
records.text: There is no stack segment. sp is an address in the core, like di, and a process starts with sp at its bot's base: the stack grows down into the free space under the body (see registers). instruction bytes does push ax 50 sp = sp - 2, then the word at sp = ax pop ax 58 ax = the word at sp, then sp = sp + 2 call label E8 rel16 push the address of the next instruction, then jump ret C3 pop an address, and jump to it Two things follow. push is a memory write and a pointer step in one byte. And call pushes an absolute address, the one thing a bot cannot know when it assembles.

records.heading: call and pop: where am I?
records.text: Every bot in this guide starts with the base idiom: call is relative, so it runs anywhere, and it pushes the address after it, which is absolute. pop takes that address off the stack. Position independence explains why a bot needs its base. The idiom leaves a trace: call wrote base + 3 into the word at base - 2, and pop does not erase it. That is one non-zero word just under the body. It is small, but a sampling scanner can land on it (see hygiene).

records.heading: push as a bomb
records.text: push ax with ax = 0 is a DAT bomb and a step of 2 in one byte. Point sp where you want to bomb, and each push zeros the next word down. Eight of them in a row, then loop, make a carpet: a zero on every byte, 16 bytes each 9 cycles. A lap zeros 65,504 bytes, every byte of the core but the 26 of the body and the 6 just over it, in 36,849 cycles. The dwarf's loop at stride 2 takes 98,271 cycles for the same carpet (stride math). The first push also zeros the word that the base idiom's call left at base - 2. A carpet with no gaps leaves an imp no gap to walk through: seeds 1..20, hill rules record Pusher vs imp 20 W / 0 T / 0 L Pusher vs imp-ring 20 W / 0 T / 0 L Pusher vs dwarf 13 W / 0 T / 7 L Pusher vs scanner 14 W / 0 T / 6 L Pusher vs paper 0 W / 8 T / 12 L Pusher vs vampire 1 W / 0 T / 19 L It loses to what a carpet cannot catch up with. Paper makes copies faster than one carpet can zero them. And eight push ax bytes in a row are code a vampire finds and bites. Try WORDS equ 1. A pass is now push ax and loop, a bomb every 2 cycles instead of 8 in 9, and a lap takes 65,519 cycles. Against the imp the record falls from 20 W / 0 T / 0 L to 16 W / 4 T / 0 L: some imps now get to the cycle cap before the carpet reaches them.

records.heading: Rules for sp tricks
records.text: sp is yours alone. Nothing else uses the stack: there are no interrupts, and no handler pushes onto it. So sp can point anywhere, and a push there is safe until your own code pushes. A bomber that uses sp cannot use call. call pushes wherever sp is, and ret pops from there. Pusher runs call once, in the base idiom, before mov sp, bx. Each process has its own sp. A child that spl starts copies the parent's sp, and from then on each moves its own. Two processes that push from the same sp bomb the same words. push sp pushes the decremented sp. That is 8086 behavior, and it is what the engine does. See also: push, pop, and call in the reference.

records.heading: What a scanner sees
records.text: Empty core is zero. A scanner cannot read who owns a byte, only the byte, so to a scanner every non-zero byte looks the same: your code, your data, your trail, your bombs if they are not zero. Hygiene is keeping the bytes a scanner can find few, small, and in one place, and making the ones you cannot hide cost it time. Two kinds of scanner look in different ways (see scanners): scanner reads finds a bot pays for a false hit byte scanner (repe scasb) every byte, one a cycle always, when the scan gets there one carpet of 16 words: 24 turns sampler (the vampire) one word in every 16 bytes only if a sampled word is in it one bite of 16 fangs: over 90 turns

records.heading: The rules
records.text: Be small. A bomb pattern with stride s hits a bot of s - 1 bytes or more on every lap, and a sampler can miss only a bot of 14 bytes or less. Each byte you cut is a byte that cannot be hit. Bomb with zeros. A zero bomb in empty core leaves no trace. A bomb that is not zero, such as the 0xCCCC of Carrier, kills as well, and leaves a trail of non-zero words that leads back toward you. Keep your data in your body. A counter or a table far from the body is a second place to find, and a second thing to lose. Clean up after the base idiom. call leaves base + 3 in the word at base - 2 (see stack tricks). mov word [bx-2], 0 costs one instruction and erases it. Make false hits cost. Non-zero bytes that are not code, a decoy, cost a scanner a carpet or a bite each. That only pays when a false hit is dear, as the numbers below show.

records.heading: A decoy
records.text: Decoy writes 1 KB of noise under its body and 1 KB over it, then bombs the core as a dwarf does. The noise is the word A1 00 over and over: mov ax, [0xa100] and then a DAT, so a process that runs into it dies within two instructions. The noise costs 1,024 turns to write, rep stosw one word a turn, before the first bomb.

records.heading: What noise buys
records.text: The same bot with 0, 1 KB, and 4 KB of noise on each side (NOISE equ 0, 1024, 4096), over 100 seeds: seeds 1..100, hill rules record Decoy, no noise vs scanner 80 W / 0 T / 20 L decoy vs scanner 80 W / 0 T / 20 L Decoy, 4 KB vs scanner 81 W / 0 T / 19 L Decoy, no noise vs vampire 22 W / 0 T / 78 L decoy vs vampire 33 W / 0 T / 67 L Decoy, 4 KB vs vampire 48 W / 0 T / 52 L Against the byte scanner, noise buys nothing. The scanner carpets 32 bytes for each hit and scans on from under the carpet, so it passes noise about as fast as empty core, and it still reaches the body. Decoy beats it for another reason: its bomber gets there first. Against the sampler, noise buys a lot. Each bite of noise is 16 fangs, over 90 turns, and it holds nothing. 4 KB of noise on each side lifts the record from 22 wins in 100 to 48. Try NOISE equ 4096: 48 wins in 100 against the vampire, where 1 KB gets 33. Open it in the arena against the vampire and watch the fangs land in the noise, bite after bite, while the bombs walk toward the vampire.

records.heading: Trails you did not mean
records.text: Imps. An imp leaves a trail of A5 90 words the whole way it walks. A stone's decoy imp is a trail on purpose; an imp you launched and forgot is a path to you. Copies. Each paper copy is a whole bot. Paper hides by number, not by size. Fangs and pits. A vampire's bite leaves 48 bytes of code in the core, and every fang holds the pit's distance. Gates. An imp gate is a word that is never zero for long, just under the body. See also: scanners, stosw, and death.

records.heading: The score in a crowd
records.text: A melee puts up to 16 bots in one core. Each round, the survivors share about N × N - 1 points (see scoring): survivors 4 bots: each scores 8 bots: each scores 1 15 63 2 7 31 3 5 21 4 3 15 Three things follow: A tie pays. In a 4-bot round, surviving with two others is 5 points, a third of a win. A duel pays a tie a third of a win too, but a melee has many more ways to tie. Each kill pays everyone left. When 3 of 4 bots are alive, a kill takes each survivor from 5 to 7. The bot that made the kill gains no more than the one that hid. Dying costs everything. A dead bot scores 0, however long it lived and whatever it killed.

records.heading: Aggression and survival
records.text: Four roster bots, 20 rounds at hill rules, order rotating as a melee match does: Vampire, Dwarf, Stone, Paper: seeds 1..20, hill rules points W T L Vampire 120 8 0 12 Paper 117 5 6 9 Stone 29 1 2 17 Dwarf 28 0 4 16 Here W counts the rounds a bot was the sole survivor, T the rounds it survived with others, and L the rounds it died. The vampire and paper come out nearly even by opposite roads. The vampire kills: it wins 8 rounds outright, and dies in 12. Paper survives: it wins 5 and ties 6. The two bombers do neither well, and score a quarter as much. A vampire in a crowd has more code to bite, and each bite turns a rival's processes against it. Paper in a crowd is everywhere, so a bomber must find it in 64 places while others bomb that bomber. open in arena loads this melee: the vampire first, then the dwarf, the stone, and paper. Try deleting the line mov word [bx+pit.hold], 0, so the pit never closes, and run the same melee. The vampire's wins fall from 8 to 0 and its points from 120 to 45: every bot it holds stays alive, so it shares every round it survives. A kill that is not finished is a tie.

records.heading: Tactics
records.text: Spread out. Many bots means many bombs from many ways. A bot with processes in more than one place, like paper, loses one at a time. Let others fight. A bot scores in every round it lives, and the last kill pays most. In a 4-bot round, the first kill takes each survivor from 3 points to 5; the last takes the winner from 7 to 15. Mind the spacing. The loader keeps bots at least 1,024 bytes apart (melee 16 halves that to 512), and 16 bots at 1 KB take a quarter of the core. Your first bombs land on someone. Count the cycles. A crowd takes longer to thin out, so the arena's melee presets run longer: 200,000 cycles for melee 8, 300,000 for melee 16. A plan that needs a whole lap has time for it. Test in the crowd you expect. The order of the bots and the seed change the result of a melee. Look at the averages over many rounds, not one battle. See also: melee tournaments, and scoring.

records.heading: How a hill scores
records.text: A hill is a standing field of bots (see hills). A new bot fights every entry, one match of several rounds each, and its score is the sum of its match points. Every entry is scored the same way against the rest of the field, so the whole field ranks on equal terms. Over the size of the hill, the lowest entry goes. Three facts decide what does well: A point is a point. A round win is 3, a tie 1, a loss 0, and they add up across every entry. Whether you won the match does not count; how many points you took from it does. Every entry counts. A bot that takes 25 of 30 from each entry scores more than one that takes 30 from half the field and 15 from the other half. The field is the other bots. Your score depends on who is on the hill. A new entry that beats you drops your score even if you never meet it again.

records.heading: A roster hill
records.text: Here is the roster's 12 fighters as one field: every pair plays a match of 10 rounds at hill rules, from seed 1, and each bot's score is the sum of its points. W, T, and L count matches. roster round robin: 10 rounds, hill rules points W T L Vampire 268 9 0 2 Paper 253 10 1 0 Silk 225 9 2 0 Hybrid 203 8 0 3 Stone 172 6 1 4 Gate 168 6 1 4 Decoy 153 4 1 6 Dwarf Wide 150 3 3 5 Dwarf 104 3 1 7 Scanner 97 2 0 9 Imp Ring 32 0 1 10 Imp 31 0 1 10 Paper loses no match, and still ranks second. Here is where the two top bots took their points: against Paper Vampire Imp 28-1 27-3 Imp Ring 18-6 28-1 Dwarf 24-3 30-0 Dwarf Wide 24-3 30-0 Gate 26-2 30-0 Decoy 26-2 27-3 Stone 24-3 24-6 Silk 10-10 3-27 Scanner 30-0 30-0 Hybrid 22-4 30-0 each other 21-9 9-21 Paper wins its matches by leaving rivals alive: a round it ties is 1 point, not 3, and it ties often, because its copies seldom finish a bot. The vampire loses badly to the two papers, but it finishes most of the rest: 30 of 30 against five of them. Its two bad matchups cost it 48 points of the 60 on offer; the finishes gave it back more.

records.heading: What the meta rewards
records.text: Finishing. A tie at the cycle cap is 1 point of 3. A bot that kills slowly, or only sometimes, bleeds points in every matchup it should win. Count what your kill needs: a whole lap at stride 4 is 49,137 cycles (see stride math), and a hill round is 80,000. No zeros. Against a bot you cannot beat, a tie is 10 points in 10 rounds where a loss is 0. Paper's 10-10 against silk is worth a third of a clean sweep. Breadth over peaks. The imps win no match and take 31 and 32 points of the 330 on offer. A bot is only as strong as its sum. The field moves. Scores are relative to the field. Take the two papers off this hill and the vampire loses no match; add two more, and its two bad matchups become four. Try deleting paper's one bomb, mov word [di+STEP/2], 0, and score the field again. Paper falls from 253 points to 222 and drops below silk: the bomb is worth 31 points across the hill. A single instruction that finishes a few more rounds matters more than a new trick.

records.heading: Reading your own score
records.text: Look at the rows, not the rank. A rank hides where the points went. Find the matchups where you tie or lose, and ask whether a change turns them without costing the others. Test against the whole field. The editor's test vs fights one roster bot for 10 rounds; a local round robin of your bot and the roster is a hill in miniature. Test with the hill's rules. Cycles, rounds, and the byte limit change what works: a 256-byte hill has no room for a long bot, and a 50,000-cycle hill has no time for a slow one. See also: hills, ratings, and scoring.

records.heading: Rounds and matches
records.text: Every format is built from the same two parts. A round is one battle. Each survivor scores floor((N * N - 1) / S) points, where N is the count of bots and S the count of survivors; a dead bot scores 0 (see scoring). A match is K rounds of the same bots. Round i uses the seed seed + i and rotates the bot order by i, so each bot goes first as often as the others. A bot's match score is the sum of its round points. A match has one winner when one bot has the most points. When two or more share the top, the match is a tie. format bots plays ranks by round robin 2 to 32 one match for each pair points, then match wins bracket 3 to 32 one match for each pair that meets, the loser out how far a bot got melee 2 to 16 one match of all the bots, in one core points, then round wins

records.heading: Round robin
records.text: Every bot fights every other bot once, one match each. With n bots that is n × (n - 1) / 2 matches: 28 for 8 bots, 66 for 12, 496 for 32. Above 12 bots the form warns about the count. The standings add up each bot's match points, and count its match wins, ties, and losses. They rank by points, then by wins, then by name. The view shows the standings and a results matrix: one row and one column for each bot, and in each cell the points the row's bot took from the column's. A round robin is the fairest format and the slowest. It is also a hill in miniature: a hill ranks its entries the same way.

records.heading: Bracket
records.text: Single elimination: a bot that loses a match is out, and the winner of the final is the champion. See brackets for seeds, byes, ties, and the third-place match.

records.heading: Melee
records.text: All the bots share one core, every round (see melee tactics). A melee is one match: K rounds, the seeds stepping and the order rotating as in any match. Each round, a bot wins if it is the only survivor, ties if it survives with others, and loses if it dies. The standings rank by points, then by round wins. A melee also keeps how long each bot lived in each round: its survival histogram puts the rounds in 10 bins from 0 to the cycle cap, and a bot that lived to the cap lands in the last bin. watch round N replays any round in the arena.

records.heading: Running a tournament here
records.text: Tournaments run in your browser. new tournament asks for: A name and a kind: round robin, bracket, or melee. The bots: roster bots, your own bots, or .asm files dropped on the form. A bot of yours is copied in with its source, so a later edit to the bot does not change the tournament. The config: rounds per match, cycles, the process cap, and the spacing, or one of the arena's presets (duel, melee 8, melee 16, hill rules). For a bracket: seeds as picked or shuffled, and the third-place match. Under the bots, the form says how many matches the tournament plays and how long it may take at most: every round run to its last cycle, at 20 million instructions a second. The matches run one at a time in the arena's Worker, headless, and the tournament is saved in this browser after every match (every round of a melee). A reload loses at most the match in flight, and the tournament goes on from where it stopped. pause and cancel stop at once and drop the match in flight.

records.heading: On the server
records.text: Tournaments lists the server's tournaments beside this browser's, each with the server chip. The server plays them as it plays a hill's submissions: one match at a time, each stored with its replay, so their standings come only from matches it ran itself. A signed-in user makes one with the API (POST /api/tournaments): its bots invited by name, or open to one entry from each player until a deadline. Its owner starts it once its entries have closed. A server tournament's page shows the same views as one run here. It joins the tournament's live room: the LIVE chip, the spectator count, and auto-watch, which plays each match here as the server starts it, then checks it against the server's result (see verification). watch on a round loads that match's replay from the server.

records.heading: The weekly championship
records.text: Every Saturday at 18:00 UTC the server starts the weekly championship: an open bracket of up to 32 bots, seeded by rating, with a third-place match, under the main hill's rules (10 rounds a match, 80,000 cycles a round, bots up to 512 bytes). Each week's is made when the last one starts, and takes entries for six days, until the Friday before it at 18:00 UTC. Sign in, and enter a version of one of your account's bots from its page or from the home page. One bot a player: enter again to swap it. The champion goes to the championships feed, the home page, and its owner's profile.

records.heading: Exports and links
records.text: export what for results.json every match with its rounds: seeds, order, points, survivors, result hashes all kinds standings CSV rank,entrant,name,points,wins,ties,losses round robin, melee bracket.svg the bracket, drawn in the page's theme bracket share a link that carries the inputs and every match played all kinds A shared tournament opens as a snapshot: the page rebuilds the standings, the bracket, and the champion from the matches in the link, so the standings cannot say what the matches do not add up to. Nothing runs it in the browser that opens it. Every match can be watched, and each round's result is checked on the way (see verification). The link format is in share links. From a shell, asmbots tourney runs the same formats (see the CLI). See also: brackets, hills, and scoring.

records.heading: Single elimination
records.text: A bracket plays matches in rounds. The two bots of a match fight one match of K rounds; the winner goes on to the next round, and the loser is out. The winner of the final is the champion. A bracket of n bots plays n - 1 matches, one more with a third-place match.

records.heading: Seeds and byes
records.text: A bracket holds 2, 4, 8, 16, or 32 places: the smallest size that holds the bots. Each bot gets a seed, 1 to n. In the first round, seed s meets seed size + 1 - s, placed so that the top seeds meet as late as they can: 8 places match 1 match 2 match 3 match 4 8 bots 1 v 8 4 v 5 2 v 7 3 v 6 6 bots 1 v bye 4 v 5 2 v bye 3 v 6 5 bots 1 v bye 4 v 5 2 v bye 3 v bye Seeds above the count of bots are byes, so the byes go to the top seeds. A match against a bye is a walkover: the bot goes on with no match run. Seeds come from one of: Seeds as picked: the order you picked the bots in. Pick the strongest first. Shuffle seeds: a random order, drawn from a seed the tournament keeps, so the same tournament shuffles the same way. Rating (the server's, as the weekly championship seeds): each bot's best rating on any hill, the highest first. A bot no hill has rated counts as 1500.

records.heading: Who goes on
records.text: A bracket match cannot end in a tie. The winner is the bot with: more match points; if level, more survival cycles, added over the match's rounds (the cycles each bot lived through in each round); if level, the better seed. So two imps that tie every round split nothing: the one that lived longer goes on, and if both lived to the cap every round, the higher seed does.

records.heading: The third-place match
records.text: With 4 or more bots, the form can add a match between the two semifinal losers. It plays in the last round, beside the final, and ranks third and fourth.

records.heading: The view
records.text: The bracket draws as columns of rounds, byes greyed, the third-place match under the final, and the champion at the right. The match in flight pulses. Click a match to open its panel: its bots with their seeds and points, and a row for each round (the seed, who fought first, the survivors, the points, the cycles) with watch, which replays that round in the arena and checks its result hash (see verification). While a tournament runs, its status chip counts the matches (running · 5 / 7). auto-watch opens each match in the arena at max speed as it starts, rebuilt from its inputs, while the runner plays it headless. bracket.svg saves the bracket as an SVG file in the page's theme. asmbots tourney bracket --svg bracket.svg draws the same bracket from a shell. See also: formats, and ratings for rating seeds.

records.heading: King of the hill
records.text: A hill is a standing field of bots: a round robin that never ends. A new bot, the challenger, fights every entry on the hill, one match each. Then the whole field, the hill and the challenger, is ranked on equal terms, and if the field is over the hill's size, the lowest bot goes. The top bot is the king. Hills run on the server. /hills lists them, with the roster bots on them from the start. Sign in, keep a bot in your account (the editor's save), and submit it from a hill's page. The rules below are the ones @asmbots/tourney runs, and the server runs the same code. To see how a bot would fare on a hill, challenge an entry in the arena: the arena plays the hill's own match. An entry whose source is private fights on the server only.

records.heading: How a challenge scores
records.text: The challenger fights each entry: one match of the hill's rounds, under the hill's rules. Each bot's score is the sum of its match points against every other bot in the field. The entries' old matches with each other are kept, not played again, so a challenge plays one match per entry. The field ranks by score. Level scores rank by age, the count of challenges a bot has stayed on the hill through: the older bot ranks higher. Level again, the old board order holds, with the challenger after every entry. If the field is over the hill's size, the lowest bot is pushed off, and its matches leave everyone's scores. Each entry that stays ages by one. So a challenger stays only if it scores more than the lowest entry, and a tie with it is not enough. A challenger with the same bytes as an entry replaces that entry: the old one and its matches go, and the challenger fights the rest and keeps the old entry's age. The server's hills refuse such a submission, since it would take another bot's place and age: change the code to challenge it. A version already on the hill is refused too.

records.heading: The hills at launch
records.text: hill entries rules main 32 duels of 10 rounds, 80,000 cycles a round, bots up to 512 bytes tiny 16 duels of 50,000 cycles a round, bots up to 256 bytes melee 8 8-bot melees of 10 rounds, scored as a melee The hill rules preset of the arena and the tournament form is main's rules: 10 rounds of 80,000 cycles.

records.heading: The hill page
records.text: A hill's page shows its standings (rank, bot, author, score, rating ± RD, W/T/L, age), king first, the king's card, the recent submissions with their deltas (+3 rank: the places a bot gained over its best version before), and the latest matches, each one a watch link. challenge on a row fights one of your bots against that entry in the arena, under the hill's rules and seed, yours first: the same match the server would play. With sign-in, submit enters a version of one of your account's bots. The server uses the bytes it assembled when you saved that version, so it never takes bytes on trust, and fights the entries one match at a time: "fighting 24 of 32". The result card gives the rank, or, if the bot does not make the hill, its score, the score it had to beat, and its closest fight. You can have one submission running on a hill at a time, and make five an hour. The melee hill takes no submissions yet. Every hill match is a match like any other, with seeds, an order, and result hashes, so you can watch any of them in the arena and check it (see verification).

records.heading: Strategy on a hill
records.text: A hill rewards points taken from every entry, not match wins; hill meta works through a hill of the roster's fighters. See also: ratings, and formats.

records.heading: What a rating is
records.text: A hill's score says how a bot did against the field on the hill now. A rating says how strong the bot is against every bot it has met, and how sure that number is. ASM BOTS rates bots with Glicko-2 (Mark Glickman), the system behind many chess and game ladders. A rating has three parts: part a new bot means rating 1500 the strength: 200 points more means an expected score of about 0.76 against the other bot RD, the rating deviation 350 the doubt: the true strength is most likely within 2 RD of the rating volatility 0.06 how much the strength itself changes over time The standings show a rating as 1612 ± 48: the rating, and the RD.

records.heading: How it moves
records.text: Ratings change once per rating period, from the games of that period. Each match between two bots is one game: the bot with more match points scores 1, the other 0; equal points score 0.5 each. In a match of more than two bots, each bot plays a game against each other bot. Plain rules follow from the math: A surprise moves more. Beat a bot rated far above you, and you gain more than for beating an equal. Doubt moves more. A bot with a high RD moves a lot on each game; a bot with a low RD barely moves. Games cut the doubt; idle time grows it. Each game lowers the RD. A period with no games leaves the rating as it was and raises the RD a little, up to 350. An opponent you know little about counts for less. A game against a bot with a high RD moves your rating less than one against a bot with a low RD.

records.heading: Examples
records.text: Each row is one rating period with one game (τ = 0.5): before the game after new, 1500 ± 350 beats 1500 ± 50 1675 ± 248 new, 1500 ± 350 beats 1700 ± 50 1805 ± 266 new, 1500 ± 350 ties 1500 ± 50 1500 ± 248 1500 ± 50 beats new, 1500 ± 350 1505 ± 51 1500 ± 50 loses to new, 1500 ± 350 1495 ± 51 1500 ± 50 no games 1500 ± 51 In the first row the new bot wins and gains 175 points. The fourth row is the same pair with the other bot winning, and the known bot gains 5. A tie between equals moves no rating, but the new bot's RD still drops from 350 to 248: it is now better known. And Glickman's own example, three games in one period: a 1500 ± 200 bot beats 1400 ± 30, and loses to 1550 ± 100 and to 1700 ± 300. After: 1464 ± 152.

records.heading: Where ratings show
records.text: Ratings belong to hills, which run on the server (see hills). On a hill, each submission is one rating period: the challenger plays a game against each entry it fought, and each of those entries a game against it. The launch seed rates the challenges that built each hill the same way. The rank on a hill comes from the score, not the rating. The rating is a second number beside it: the bot's strength over its whole history on that hill, and its bot page draws it as a line over time. A bracket can seed by rating: the highest rating gets seed 1. The code is updateRating and rateMatches in @asmbots/tourney. Its test runs Glickman's example to the decimal. See also: hill meta, and brackets.

records.heading: Every result can be run again
records.text: A battle is a pure function: the same bots, the same config, and the same seed give the same battle, cycle for cycle, on every machine. The engine reads no clock and no random source. The only chance in a battle is where the loader puts the bots, and that comes from the seed (see placement and seeds). So a result needs no trust. Anyone with the inputs can run the battle again and get the same end. That is what makes a share link, a replay, and a tournament snapshot worth something: each carries the inputs, and the page that opens it plays them.

records.heading: The result hash
records.text: The engine sums up a battle's end as a result: the cycles it ran, the survivors, and for each bot its name, whether it lived, its points, the cycle and reason of its death, and its counts (processes, peak processes, instructions, writes, and the bytes it owns). The result hash is FNV-1a 64 over that result as canonical JSON (keys sorted, no spaces): 16 hex digits. The dwarf against the imp at hill rules, seed 1, ends at cycle 16,141 with the dwarf alone, and hashes to 22bea637e0bb3afa. Two runs that end the same way give the same hash; a change anywhere in the end gives another. A replay, a tournament's results.json, and a shared tournament record one result hash for each round. The engine also hashes a battle's whole event stream, every instruction, write, spawn, and death. The test suite plays the roster's 152 golden rounds in Bun on the main thread and in a Worker, and checks both hashes against the stored ones. The same inputs give the same event hash, byte for byte, or the build fails.

records.heading: The verified chip
records.text: A replay page (/arena/<match key>#r=…, the link that replay link copies) plays the replay's match in the arena and checks it as it goes: The bots. Each bot's bytes must hash to the SHA-256 the replay records. The match. The arena's match key, a hash of the config, the round count, and each bot's name and bytes, must equal the replay's. Each round. When a round ends, its result hash must equal the recorded one. chip means verifying no round has ended yet verified 1/3 one round of three matched; the rest are still running verified every round matched, the bots matched their SHA-256, and the match key matched mismatch one check failed; the chip's title, and the victory, say which A mismatch names what failed: bytes that do not match their SHA-256, a replay that would not run, a match of other bots or another config (a changed setting is a mismatch even if the result happens to agree), or a round whose result hash differs from the one recorded. The chip checks the arena's own run. It is not a second simulation, and it proves the same thing: these inputs give this result, here, now.

records.heading: Tournaments
records.text: watch on a round of a tournament rebuilds that round from its inputs (the bots in the round's order, and the round's seed), plays it in the arena, and shows the same chip: verified when the result hash matches the one the tournament recorded. A shared tournament carries every match's rounds with their hashes, so anyone who opens the link can watch and check any round. A server tournament's round comes from the match's replay, which the server stored with the bots' bytes: the arena checks it the same way.

records.heading: Live matches
records.text: A hill's page joins the hill's live room, and a server tournament's page the tournament's. When the server starts a match there, the room sends the match's inputs: each bot's name, bytes, and SHA-256, the config, the seed, and the round count. With auto-watch on, the page's arena plays that match at max speed, one round after another: you watch the battle the server is running, run on your machine. When the match ends on the server, the room sends the result the server stored, with each round's result hash. The chip under the arena then works as a replay's does: verifying until your run and the server's result are both in, verified when the bots match their SHA-256, the match key matches, and each round's hash matches, and mismatch when one check fails. A board only changes from matches the server ran itself, and anyone who watches checks them.

records.heading: Verify any match
records.text: A match you did not watch can be checked too. Every match the server played has verify beside it: in the recent matches of the home page and of each hill (the main hill, say), in a submission's matches, and in a server tournament's match panel. verify asks the server for the match with GET /api/matches/<match id>/verify. The answer has two parts: The inputs: each bot's name, bytes, and SHA-256, the config, the seed, and the round count, as the match's replay stored them, with the match key the server recorded. The result: the match's row, the one the standings came from, with its result hash and each round's. Your browser then plays the rounds in an arena Worker, one after another, with nothing drawn, and the chip takes the button's place: chip means verifying no round has ended yet verified 2/10 two rounds of ten matched; the rest are still running verified the bots matched their SHA-256, the match key matched, and every round's result hash matched the server's mismatch one check failed; the chip's title says which, and no round after it runs The hills' first matches, the ones the launch seed played, recorded one hash for the whole match, not one a round: their chip says verifying until the last round ends, then checks that one hash. The server takes no part in the check. It hands over what it ran, and your machine decides.

records.heading: What verification does not cover
records.text: That a bot is the one a person wrote. A replay proves what these bytes do. Names and sources are labels; the SHA-256 is of the bytes. A different ISA. A replay records x16c-v1. The arena refuses a replay of another ISA version rather than run it under the wrong rules (see ISA versions). See also: the replay format, and share links.

records.heading: Install
records.text: asmbots is the command line of ASM BOTS: the same assembler, engine, and tournament code as the web app, in a shell. It runs on Bun. From a clone of the repository: Or, with no link, from the repository root: bun apps/cli/src/main.ts <command> …. Each command takes --help. A bot is a roster slug (roster:dwarf), an .asm file (assembled first), or a .bin file (raw bytes). Color is off with --no-color, with --json, when NO_COLOR is set, or when the output is not a terminal. exit code means 0 done 1 usage: a missing argument, an unknown command or format, or a --trace-bot name that no bot has 2 asm: the source has errors 3 a runtime error: a file that cannot be read, a bot that does not assemble, or an unknown roster slug

records.heading: asm
records.text: Assembles a source file and prints each diagnostic as file:line:col: severity: message [code], the form editors turn into links, then the size: --listing prints each line's address and bytes beside its source. --bin writes the bytes to a file; without it, nothing is written. --max-bytes fails the build of a bot over that size (the arena's limit is 512).

records.heading: dis
records.text: Disassembles raw bytes, one instruction a line: address, bytes, and NASM text that assembles back to the same bytes. --base is the address of the first byte, in hex, so jump targets read as the core's addresses. A byte that is not a defined instruction prints as db 0xNN, and 00 as dat.

records.heading: fight
records.text: Runs a battle and prints where each bot was placed, the survivors, and each bot's counts: instructions, writes, peak processes, points, and the cycle and reason of its death. With no --seed, the seed is random. --cycles, --procs, and --spacing set the cycle cap, the process cap, and the least gap between two bots. --json prints the engine's result as JSON, with the trace lines: the same result that the result hash hashes. --trace prints a line for each bot each cycle: the cycle, the bot, the process, the address and bytes of the instruction, then ax, cx, dx, bx, si, di, bp, and sp, and the flags as cpazstido (a capital letter for a flag that is set). --trace-bot "Dwarf" keeps one bot's lines. The screen shows the first 100 lines; --json holds them all.

records.heading: tourney
records.text: Runs a tournament of the bots at the engine's default config (see formats) and prints the standings, or a bracket's champion. --rounds is the rounds per match. --out writes the results as JSON: the standings of a round robin or a melee, or a whole bracket with every match's rounds (seed, order, points, and result hash). --svg writes a bracket as an SVG file. The seed is random on each run.

records.heading: bench
records.text: Runs battles of two dwarves for that long and prints the engine's speed in instructions a second. Known gaps in this build: fight --rounds K runs K rounds with the seeds seed to seed + K - 1, but it does not rotate the bot order as a match does, and it prints only the last round. For a match, use tourney roundrobin with two bots. tourney has no --seed, and only a bracket's --out file records the seeds it used. hill submit does not work: the second bot fails with "is 8192 bytes, not 1..512". Hills arrive with the server. golden runs bun run golden, which it finds only at the repository root: run it there. --json does nothing for asm and dis. See also: the replay format, and verification.

records.heading: What a replay holds
records.text: A replay is a match as the arena played it: everything it takes to run the match again, and what came out, so anyone can run it and compare (see verification). It is JSON. The arena writes it two ways: download replay saves a file, asmbots-<bots>-<seed>.asmreplay.json: the bots' names, lowercase with dashes (or 8-bots past three), and the seed. For example asmbots-dwarf-imp-1.asmreplay.json. The file keeps each bot's source where the arena had it. replay link copies a link to /arena/<match key>#r=<replay>: the same JSON, sources left out, as base64url in the link's fragment. The page it opens plays the match and checks it. The app cannot open a replay file yet. A replay link carries the same inputs.
