records.heading: The fields
records.text: field holds isa x16c-v1: the instruction set the bots are written for (see ISA versions) createdAt optional: when the replay was made, ISO 8601 config the battle config, every field written out, less the seed seed the match's first seed: round i is placed with seed + i, mod 2^32 rounds rounds in the match, 1 to 10 bots 2 to 16 bots, in the order they were loaded bots[].name the name in the battle: Dwarf, or Dwarf 2 for a second dwarf bots[].bytes the machine code, standard base64 bots[].sha256 SHA-256 of the machine code, lowercase hex bots[].meta optional: author, strategy, version bots[].source optional: the source; a file has it, a link does not result.key the match key: FNV-1a 64 of the config, the seed, the round count, and each bot's name and bytes result.survivors the bots alive at the end of the last round, ascending, as indices into bots result.points each bot's match points, in bots order result.resultHash one hash for the match: FNV-1a 64 of the JSON list of the rounds' result hashes, in order result.rounds[] one entry for each round, in order Each round: field holds round its number, from 0 seed its placement seed: the match seed plus round, mod 2^32 order the fighting order: order[j] is the bot placed j-th, as an index into bots. Round i rotates the order by i. resultHash the result hash of the round's battle, with the bots in fighting order durationCycles the cycles the battle ran points each bot's round points, in bots order survivors the bots alive at the end, ascending, as indices into bots survival the cycles each bot lived through: its death cycle, or durationCycles if it lived A replay's content key, the name the server stores it by, is the SHA-256 of its inputs as canonical JSON (keys sorted, no whitespace): isa, config, seed, rounds, and each bot's name and bytes. The result, the sources, and the date do not change it.

records.heading: Checks and limits
records.text: The arena reads a replay only if every field is there and well formed. It refuses one of another isa, one with a count out of range (2 to 16 bots, 1 to 10 rounds, up to 1,000,000 cycles, up to 256 processes a bot), and a link whose replay is over 1,048,576 characters. Then it plays the match and checks it as verification describes: the bytes against their SHA-256, the match key, and each round's result hash. Before this format, the arena wrote asmbots-replay-local/1: the seed inside config, and match (with names and of) where result is now. The arena still reads those files and links. See also: share links, and the CLI, whose fight --json prints the same engine result that a round's hash covers.

records.heading: The URL is the state
records.text: A link in ASM BOTS carries what it shows. There is no server to look it up in: the query names the settings, and the fragment (after #) carries anything bigger, such as your bots' sources. A browser does not send a fragment to the server, so the source of your unsaved bot stays between you and the person you send the link to. Every link that runs a battle carries its inputs, so the battle it shows is the battle you saw (see verification). link copied by opens /arena?b=…&seed=… copy a share link in the arena setup, share on the victory the arena, set up to fight /arena/<match key>#r=… replay link on the victory a replay, checked as it plays /editor#src=… share in the editor the source, as a bot not saved yet /editor/roster-dwarf share on a roster bot that roster bot /tournaments/<id>#t=… share on a tournament the tournament, as a snapshot

records.heading: Arena links
records.text: The query names the bots and the config: key holds b the bots, in order, comma-separated: roster:<slug> for a roster bot, local:<id> for a bot of the sharer's browser. Up to 16. seed the seed of the first round, 0 to 4,294,967,295. Left out, or out of range, each battle draws a random one. cycles the cycle cap, 10,000 to 1,000,000 rounds rounds per match, 1 to 10 procs the process cap, 1 to 256 spacing the least gap between bots, 0 to 8,192 bytes A field left out takes its duel value, so a link means the same battle in every browser. Any other value out of range is held to the range. The one exception is /arena with no query at all: that opens the setup you last used. A local: bot is in no other browser, so the link carries its source in the fragment: #src= and the base64url of the deflated JSON [[id, source], …]. The page that opens the link loads each local: bot from there.

records.heading: Editor links
records.text: share in the editor copies /editor#src=…, the same fragment with one bot. It opens the source as a bot not saved yet; save it to keep it. A roster bot needs no source in the link: its link is its page, /editor/roster-<slug>. Every open in editor and open in arena button of these docs is one of these links. The editor also reads two queries: ?t=dwarf starts a new bot from a template, and the arena's open in debugger sends its ?b=…&seed=…, which opens the first bot in the debugger against the others.

records.heading: Replay links
records.text: /arena/<match key>#r= and the base64url of the replay's JSON, sources left out. The replay format has every field. The page plays the match and shows the verified chip.

records.heading: Tournament links
records.text: /tournaments/<id>#t= and the base64url of the tournament's deflated JSON (format asmbots-tournament-link/1): its name, kind, status, config, rounds, seeding, and entrants, and every match it played. A roster bot travels as its slug. A bot of yours travels as its machine code, so its rounds can be watched from the link. A browser that has no tournament by that id opens the link as a snapshot: the page rebuilds the standings, the bracket, and the champion from the matches, and runs nothing. A tournament that was running when it was shared reads as paused.

records.heading: Embeds
records.text: share ▾ then copy embed copies an <iframe> of a battle, to paste into another site. Its address is the arena link under /embed: /embed/arena?b=…#src=… for a battle, /embed/arena/<key> for a stored replay. The embed shows the arena alone, plays as it loads, and links back with watch on asmbots. It makes no sound and takes no keys, so the page around it keeps its own.

records.heading: Cards
records.text: A link to a replay, a bot, a hill, a tournament, or a docs page shows a card where it is shared: a 1200 × 630 picture the server draws from the data (the core at a replay's end, a bot's identicon, a hill's standings, a bracket). share ▾ then download png saves it.

records.heading: Size
records.text: Links are long when they carry sources, and some chat apps cut long links. A share link holds up to 16 bots of 16 KB of source each, and a replay link up to about 1 MB. If a link opens with its bots missing, it was cut: share it another way, or share the .asm files. See also: the replay format, and verification.

records.heading: Every key
records.text: The table below is drawn from the same list the pages register their keys from, so it is always the app's keys. Press ? on any page for the keys that work there now; the settings page lists them too.

records.heading: How keys work
records.text: One key or a chord. g a is a chord: g, then a within 600 ms. When one key is both a command and the start of a chord, the command runs at once. Text fields keep their keys. While a field or the source editor has the focus, the letters and the punctuation are your typing, not commands. esc leaves the source editor, so the page keys work again. The browser keeps its combinations. Keys with ctrl, alt, or cmd belong to the browser, except the source editor's own and mod+s in the editor. mod is cmd on macOS and ctrl elsewhere. Function keys work anywhere in the editor. F5 to F11 drive the debugger even while you type, and never reach the browser (F5 would reload the page). space goes to the focused control first. On a button or a checkbox it presses that control; elsewhere it plays and pauses. Route keys come and go. The arena's keys work while a battle shows, and 1 to 9 reach as many bots as the battle has. A route's key wins over a global key with the same name while the route shows. The source editor also has CodeMirror's usual keys: mod+z to undo, mod+f to find, and the rest. See also: the debugger tour, and start here.

records.heading: api
records.text: The API is not live yet. It arrives with the server: the hills, accounts, cloud bots, and stored replays. This page will list its routes then. Until it does, everything in ASM BOTS runs in your browser, and the CLI runs the same code in a shell.

records.heading: What is planned
records.text: A read API first, then writes behind sign-in: route gives GET /api/health the server's version and ISA GET /api/bots/:id a bot, and its versions GET /api/replays/:key a stored replay, in the replay format's shared successor GET /api/hills, GET /api/hills/:slug the hills, and a hill's standings GET /api/tournaments/:id a tournament POST /api/assemble the bytes and the diagnostics of a source, assembled on the server POST /api/replays stores a replay after the server has run it again and checked its result hashes Errors will come as { "error": { "code", "message" } }. The server runs the same engine and the same tournament code as the browser, so a result from the API is one you can run again here (see verification). See also: share links, which work with no server at all.

records.heading: changelog
records.text: Every release of ASM BOTS, newest first. A release is named by its date, YYYY.MM.DD, with a letter for each release of that day (2026.10.03a), and has a name of its own from Core War lore. The version chip in the status bar is the build you run: point at it for its release. The instruction set has its own version, which changes far less often: see ISA versions.

records.heading: 2026.09.25a · "imp gate"
records.text: ASM BOTS v3 is a new build from the ground up. Its instruction set, x16c, is real 8086 machine code, and the arena, the editor, the debugger, and local tournaments run in your browser. The machine x16c v1: a 64 KB core of bytes, one flat address space, 8086 encoding with three documented divergences (DAT, SPL, no segments). One codec encodes and decodes every instruction, so the assembler, the disassembler, the engine, and the debugger cannot disagree about an instruction. The engine: processes, spl, the process cap, rep one iteration a cycle, owner tags for every byte, and a determinism contract. A battle is a pure function of its bots, its config, and its seed, with a result hash and an event hash to prove it. The assembler: NASM syntax, local labels, equ and %define, times, expressions, and diagnostics that name the fix. A disassembler whose output assembles back to the same bytes, a formatter, and a linter. The roster 14 fighters and painters in six classic families (imp, dwarf, stone, paper, scanner, vampire) and a painter family of its own, plus 8 test bots. Each fighter's header records its fights, and 152 golden rounds pin what the roster does. Tournaments Rounds, matches, round robins, melees of up to 16 bots, single-elimination brackets, King of the Hill, pMARS scoring, and Glicko-2 ratings, in one package that the browser, the CLI, and the server share. The app The arena: up to 16 bots, WebGL2 with a 2D fallback, a transport with step back, the events log, the victory, share links, and replays with the verified chip. The editor: the x16c mode with the listing gutter, lint as you type, format, test vs, versions, and a debugger with registers, processes, memory, watches, breakpoints, a trace, 256 steps back, and an arena strip. Local tournaments: brackets, round robins, and melees, saved after every match, with exports and snapshot links. Five themes, a keyboard for everything, and these docs: the machine, a language reference generated from the opcode table, the strategy guide, and every code block runnable. The asmbots CLI: asm, dis, fight, tourney, and bench. The server Sign in with GitHub: a handle, cloud bots with versions, and a profile. Hills: submit a bot, and the server fights it against every entry, ranks the field, and rates it with Glicko-2. The board keeps the best, and its feed says what each challenge did. Server tournaments and the weekly championship, watched live, with every published match verifiable in your browser. Share cards for replays, bots, hills, and tournaments; the arena as an embed; and an API. Polish Opt-in sound, the arena tour and a guided intro, empty and error states, and an offline banner. Accessibility: no axe violation in any theme, every flow by keyboard alone, and a live region for the arena. Budgets for the cold load and the frame rate. Details that come with age: release names on the version chip, an fps chip that names the fix when frames drop, arena screenshots signed with their bots, seed, cycle, and site, first seen and fights on a bot's page, the king's reign on a hill, uptime in /api/health, and an imp on the 404 page and in robots.txt.

records.heading: Before v3
records.text: ASM BOTS v1 (2025) and v2 (April 2026) were earlier tries at the same game with a made-up instruction set. Their bots never truly ran, and v3 keeps only their look and their ideas.

records.heading: x16c v1: frozen
records.text: The instruction set is a contract between the assembler, the engine, the debugger, and every bot ever written. It has a version, and the current one, x16c v1, is frozen: no change to what a byte does, however small, goes in under this name. The status bar shows the ISA the engine runs (x16c v1), and every replay records it ("isa": "x16c-v1"). The arena refuses a replay of another ISA rather than run it under the wrong rules. part x16c v1 core 65,536 bytes, one flat address space; every address and value wraps registers ax bx cx dx si di bp sp, their 8-bit halves, ip, and the flags CF PF AF ZF SF DF OF instructions the 8086 subset in the language reference, 1 to 6 bytes, every one 1 cycle processes a queue for each bot, 64 by default; spl at the cap does nothing death DAT (00), hlt, int3, an undefined opcode, or a divide error battle turn order rotating each cycle; placement from a PCG32 seed, 1,024 bytes apart or more by default scoring pMARS: floor((N * N - 1) / S) for each of S survivors divergences from the 8086 three: 00 is DAT, 60..62 are SPL, and no segments, interrupts, I/O, or timing (divergences)

records.heading: What makes a new version
records.text: Any change to what a bot does: an opcode, a flag, a cycle cost, the process model, placement, or scoring. Even a flag fix. A new version: gets a new name, x16c v2, and a note here that says what changed and why; comes with new goldens: the roster's recorded rounds are played again, and every changed round is explained; may re-run a hill's standings, since old results were won under old rules. A change to the tools that leaves every byte doing the same thing is not a new ISA: a new diagnostic, a new directive that assembles to the same bytes, a faster engine that gives the same hashes. The goldens prove the last one: a faster engine must give the same event hash for every golden round.

records.heading: Changes since the freeze
records.text: None. One clarification. The ISA text says push sp pushes "the pre-decrement value (8086 behavior)". Those two disagree: the 8086 pushes sp after it takes 2 away, and the 80286 and later push the value from before. The engine does what the 8086 does, as the text's intent is, and the reference documents it: See also: changelog, and verification for how a replay records the ISA.
